chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) who said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to me who said: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid narrated to me, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abdullah ibn Sin'an who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: God, may His Majesty be Exalted, said:

"I have given the world among My servants as a loan. Whoever lends Me from it a loan, I will give him for each one of them ten to seven hundred times, and whatever I will from that. And whoever does not lend Me from it a loan, I will take from him by force, and I will give him three qualities: if one of them were given to My angels, they would be pleased: Salat (prayer/blessings), Guidance, and Mercy."
Indeed God, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Those who, when a calamity befalls them, say: Indeed we belong to God and indeed to Him we return. Those are upon whom are blessings from their Lord.'
One of the three is 'and mercy', two are 'and those are the guided', three [are blessings/prayers],
Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: This is for the one from whom God took something by force.

key_terms.الصَّلَاةَ: blessings or prayers (in this context, distinct from ritual prayer)

ai.seo_question: What are the three spiritual rewards God gives to those who give charity even if forced?
ai.summary: In *Al-Khisal*, Shaykh al-Saduq presents this Qudsi hadith to illustrate the spiritual economics of charity, distinguishing between voluntary generosity and compelled giving. While voluntary charity yields exponential divine reward, even reluctant giving secures three key spiritual benefits—Salat (divine blessings), Hidayah (guidance), and Rahmah (mercy)—which al-Saduq explicitly links to the tripartite reward promised to the patient in Surah Al-Baqarah. This underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the intrinsic value of enduring calamity with patience, regardless of the giver's initial disposition.
